new.headline: You ran 3:50, which is 12 minutes faster than your first marathon, and you held goal pace for 20 miles. This week is rest and walking, plus two short easy runs at the weekend only if your quads handle stairs normally.

flags.title: Quads on stairs
flags.detail: Only run on Saturday if stairs feel normal. If they still hurt, walk instead and try again a day or two later.

flags.title: Left big toe blister
flags.detail: Don't run until it no longer changes how you land. Protecting it can push the strain somewhere else.

flags.title: Sleep
flags.detail: You averaged 6.5 hours in race week, down from your usual 7 to 7.5. Get back to that this week, because most of the repair happens overnight.

flags.title: Heart rate on the first runs
flags.detail: Expect it to run higher than usual at easy pace. Keep it under 140, and slow down or walk rather than chase your normal 9:50/mi.

flags.title: Your next goal
flags.detail: Tell me in your next check-in whether the Thanksgiving 10K is on and what you want after it.

answers.question: How long before I can run again? A friend wants me to race the Thanksgiving 10K in five weeks.
answers.answer:
You can try your first run on Sat Oct 24, six days after the race, if stairs feel normal and the blister doesn't change how you land. Until then, rest and walking do more for your recovery than running would. If Saturday still feels off, walk instead and try again a day or two later.

The Thanksgiving 10K on Thu Nov 26 is a good next race, and the timing works. It's five and a half weeks after the marathon. That gives you two easy weeks, then about three weeks with one faster session each, then an easy race week. Run it as a hard effort that's also fun. We can set a time goal once the faster sessions show where your fitness is. Tell me in your next check-in if you're in, and I'll build the plan toward it.

new.analysis:
## Race week
You ran race week exactly as planned. Every run hit its distance, and Wednesday's 2 miles at marathon pace came in at 8:34/mi, right on target. Your hard minutes jumped, only 33% of your time was easy and your weekly report warned of overload. The race caused all three, so there's nothing to fix.

## The race
You paced the first 20 miles for a 3:45, and your legs gave out before your heart and lungs did. Your heart rate climbed only 6.5 bpm over the whole race, so your aerobic fitness held up. You slowed when your quads went.

| Section | Pace |
| --- | --- |
| Goal pace for 3:45 | 8:35/mi |
| First 20 mi | about 8:32/mi |
| Last 10K | about 9:28/mi |
| First half | 8:32/mi |
| Second half | 8:58/mi |

Three things probably caused the fade. The race moved two weeks earlier, so you got one 20-miler instead of the full build. Your long runs were all steady at about 10:00/mi with no marathon-pace miles. That means your legs never practiced goal pace late in a long run. The course also climbed 617 ft, more than any of your training runs, and the downhills are hard on quads.

You still took 12 minutes off on a shortened build, and that's real progress. For the next marathon, the fix is clear. Run more long runs of 18 to 22 miles, put marathon-pace miles in some of them, train on hillier routes, and keep up strength work through the whole build.

## Why this week looks like this
A marathon damages your muscles, and that damage lasts longer than the soreness does. That's why this week is mostly rest and walking, and the two weekend runs are optional tests of your legs. I've capped them by heart rate rather than pace, because heart rate often runs high for a week or two after a marathon. If it does, slowing down is the right response.

Next week, Oct 26 – Nov 1, adds more easy running, about 15 to 20 miles if this week goes well. Save strides and faster running for early November, once your legs have had two full weeks.

## What comes next
Tell me in your next check-in what you want after this. The Thanksgiving 10K, a spring marathon or a few relaxed weeks of easy base running are all good choices. Each would shape November differently, so I'll plan around whichever you pick.

safetyCallouts.title: Watch for soreness that changes.
safetyCallouts.body: General quad and calf soreness should ease a little every day. If pain settles in one spot, gets worse or makes you limp, stop running and see a physio or doctor.

safetyCallouts.title: Keep an eye on the blister.
safetyCallouts.body: If your left big toe gets red, swollen or warm, or the blister starts to leak, have a doctor or pharmacist look at it before you run.
